narrative:
Based on a predictive model, your chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt was estimated at 66.3 percent. This high probability is why your law school application was denied. The most influential factor by far was your class ranking in your third year. You sit in the bottom decile, meaning you ranked among the lowest students in your year group, while accepted applicants typically land around the sixth decile. This steep decline in your academic standing during a period of increasingly complex coursework sent a strong signal toward failure, because third-year performance often mirrors readiness for the bar.

Two other factors pushed slightly in the opposite direction, toward passing, but their influence was weak compared to your third-year rank. Your first-year decile of five is close to the accepted average of six, showing a reasonable start, and your LSAT score of 34, though below the average of about 37, still functioned as a modest positive signal. Together, these could not outweigh the overwhelming concern raised by your bottom-of-class performance in your final year. The model essentially saw a student whose earlier promise faded dramatically, predicting that this trend would continue into the bar exam.

Your best next step is to directly address that weakness: consider retaking low third-year courses or pursuing additional advanced coursework to demonstrate you can handle rigorous legal material. Strongly prepare for an LSAT retake to raise your score into a more competitive range, and then seek an individual review of your file, presenting these improvements alongside any recent achievements or a compelling personal statement. That evidence would give the admissions committee a reason to look beyond the model’s warning.
